warmup.q: Two copies of the payments program receive the same payment message at the same moment. Each one asks the database whether it already has a payment with the message's code (SELECT ... WHERE payment_uid = ?), and if it finds nothing, adds the payment (INSERT). The code column is marked UNIQUE, a rule that no two rows may share a code. What happens?
options: The second program's question waits for the first program's insert, so it sees the payment and skips it
Both questions find nothing. The second insert waits for the first program to finish, then fails with an error: that code already exists
Both inserts succeed, because each check passed
The database combines the two inserts into one row
warmup.why: A question (a SELECT) never waits for another program's unfinished insert. It sees only changes that have been saved for good, so both programs find nothing. The UNIQUE rule is what notices. The second insert finds the first one's new entry, not yet saved, and waits to see whether it will be. Once it is, the second insert fails with a duplicate key error, code 23505. So the data stays right, but one program got an error instead of an answer. Without the UNIQUE rule, the third option is what you'd get: one coffee stored twice. The third section plays this race frame by frame.

sections.h: Storing a document whose shape keeps changing: jsonb
sections.html:
Let's set up the app first. A small company runs the program that records card payments for cafés, bookshops and grocers. It keeps its data in PostgreSQL, a free database program. A database keeps data in tables, like the sheets of a spreadsheet: named columns, and one row per record. SQL is the language for asking tables questions and changing them: a SELECT statement asks a question and returns rows, and an INSERT adds a row.

The payments table has one row per payment. Its columns say which card paid (card_id), which shop was paid (merchant_id: the labs call a shop a merchant, and keep the shops in merchants), how much in cents (amount_minor), whether the money has moved (status) and when (created_at).

Every payment is also checked for fraud. A fraud check is a program that scores each payment from 0 to 100 for how suspicious it looks, and lists the rules that fired. The rule velocity, for example, fires when one card pays many times in a few minutes. The fraud team adds a field every month or so, and a column for each would mean changing the table every month. So the column metadata holds the fraud check's answer as it arrived, as JSON:

{"channel": "web", "risk": {"score": 91, "rules": ["velocity"]}}

JSON is a common way to write structured data as text. Curly braces hold an object: named values, each written as a key and its value ("channel" is a key, "web" its value). Square brackets hold a list, called an array. So this payment was made on a website and scored 91, because the velocity rule fired.

Stored as plain text, the document means nothing to PostgreSQL. A document cut off halfway is stored without complaint. Every question becomes a search for letters: metadata LIKE '%velocity%' (LIKE matches a pattern, and % stands for any characters) also matches a rule called velocity_hourly, or a note that mentions the word.

The jsonb type parses the text when you store it: it reads the text once, works out its structure, and refuses anything that isn't valid JSON. It keeps the result as a tree of keys and values, so a query can go straight to risk, then to score. An older type, json, keeps the exact text, with its spaces, its key order and any key written twice. jsonb tidies it: keys come back in its own order, and of two equal keys only the last survives. Use jsonb unless you must hand back the exact text you were sent.

On paper, plain text is a handwritten note stapled to a line of the café's order book: to find the score, you read the whole note. jsonb is the same note on a printed form with a box labelled "score".

Two operators, symbols that act on values, take you inside a document. -> takes a key, or a position in an array, and returns jsonb: still a piece of document. ->> does the same and returns text. So metadata -> 'risk' -> 'score' is the JSON number 91, and metadata -> 'risk' ->> 'score' is the text '91'.

The difference bites when you compare. Text is compared letter by letter, the way a dictionary sorts words, so '8' > '50' is true: '8' comes after '5'. The lab database starts with a small seed data set, 37 payments you can check by hand, and 8 of them score above 50. metadata -> 'risk' ->> 'score' > '50' finds 14, because six of them score from 6 to 9. Turn the text into a number before you compare: (metadata -> 'risk' ->> 'score')::int > 50, where ::int means "read this as a whole number", finds the right 8.

The operator to know best is containment, @>. metadata @> '{"risk": {"rules": ["velocity"]}}' asks whether the document contains that smaller document: a risk object whose rules array holds "velocity", whatever else is around it. It finds payments 3, 15 and 18, and never a rule that merely starts with the same letters. Its cousin ? asks whether a key, or a text item in an array, exists: metadata -> 'risk' -> 'rules' ? 'velocity'.

On a million payments, though, containment still reads every one. Next, we'll make it fast.

aside.title: Why not keep the whole payment in one JSON document?
aside.html: It's tempting: the table would never need to change. But a column gets a type and rules that PostgreSQL checks on every write. amount_minor must be a whole number above zero, status must be one of three words, and card_id must name a card that exists. Inside a document, nothing checks any of that, so a misspelled status goes in without a word. Keep the facts every payment has in real columns, and use jsonb for the part whose shape keeps changing. The Data models track asks this question properly, starting with what tables make hard.

sections.h: Finding 478 documents out of a million with a GIN index
sections.html:
Let's try containment on a bigger table. The lab's large data set holds a million made-up payments in a schema called big, a named group of tables inside the database. Among them the lab planted 478 near-copies of other payments, each marked in its document with "injected_dup": true. Finding them with metadata @> '{"injected_dup": true}' takes from half a second to a few seconds, depending on how busy your laptop is.

Where does the time go? PostgreSQL stores a table on disk in blocks of 8 KB, called pages. With no better way to find the rows, it reads every page, first to last, and tests every row: a sequential scan. This table has 23,818 pages, 186 MB, and the query reads all of them to return 478 rows. EXPLAIN (ANALYZE) shows it: it runs the query and reports the plan, the steps PostgreSQL chose to answer it, with the time of each step and the pages it touched (the Buffers line).

The usual fix is an index, a separate structure that finds rows without reading the whole table. The kind the last lesson used for paging, called a B-tree, keeps values sorted like the names in a phone book, so it finds one value or a range quickly. It can't help here: "contains this key somewhere inside" isn't a value or a range in a sorted list of whole documents.

What helps is the index at the back of a book: every word, with the pages it appears on. Look up two words, and read only the pages listed under both. A GIN index (generalized inverted index) is exactly that. For every key and every value that occurs in any document, it keeps a sorted list of the rows that contain it. For @>, PostgreSQL looks up each key and value of the smaller document, keeps the rows that appear in every list, and reads only those. The figure shows three documents and some of their entries.

CREATE INDEX payments_metadata_gin ON payments USING gin (metadata) takes a few seconds to build, and the index is under 9 MB, against 186 MB for the table. Now the same query reads 17 pages: 3 of the index, and the 14 table pages where the 478 rows live. It takes under a millisecond. EXPLAIN calls this a Bitmap Index Scan: PostgreSQL first collects the matching rows from the index, then fetches them from the table.

The book picture also explains the plan's Recheck Cond line. A book's index says page 40 has both "risk" and "velocity", not whether they share a sentence. The default GIN index, too, records keys and values but not how they nest, so PostgreSQL checks each row it fetches against the full condition.

The index has two limits. First, it serves only the jsonb operators: @>, ? and four relatives (?|, ?&, @?, @@). metadata ->> 'injected_dup' = 'true' asks the same question as the containment query and still reads every page, because the index holds keys and values, not the text that ->> makes from them. Write containment.

Second, an index helps only when it lets PostgreSQL read less. The velocity rule fired on 5% of the payments: 50,188 rows spread over 21,036 of the 23,818 pages. Counting them through the GIN index was slower than the sequential scan, because it visited almost every page anyway, after a trip through the index.

Next, we'll start writing rows, and meet a bug that no index can find.

sections.h: Check first, then insert: how one message gets stored twice
sections.html:
Back to the opening's café. Each payment reaches the company as a message, and a sender that hears no answer sends the message again. That rule is called at-least-once delivery: every message arrives, and some arrive twice. The company runs two copies of its program, called workers, so that one can carry on if the other crashes. A copy sent again can reach the second worker while the first is still storing the original.

To tell a repeat from a new payment, the card reader gives every payment a long unique code, payment_uid, and a copy sent again carries the same code. A code like that is an idempotency key: it lets the receiver spot a repeat. (Idempotent means that doing something twice has the same effect as doing it once.) The obvious code looks first:

if (payments.findByUid(msg.uid) == null) {     // both workers: not found
    payments.insert(msg)                       // both workers: insert
}

Two workers can both run the check before either inserts. Both find nothing, and both insert. With nothing else in the way, one payment would be stored twice, and the shop paid twice.

Something does stop it here. The payment_uid column is marked UNIQUE, a rule that no two rows may share a value. PostgreSQL keeps that rule with a unique index: a sorted list of every code in the column, which every insert must pass through.

A transaction is a group of changes that the database applies all together or not at all. BEGIN starts one, COMMIT saves its changes for good and shows them to everyone else, and ROLLBACK throws them away. Until a worker commits, no other worker can see its new row.

Now replay the race. Worker A inserts, and its new code goes into the unique index at once, marked as belonging to A's unfinished transaction. Worker B's insert reaches the index and finds an entry for the same code. B can't know yet whether A will commit, so it waits. If A commits, B's insert fails with duplicate key value violates unique constraint. Every PostgreSQL error carries a five-character code called a SQLSTATE, and this one's is 23505. If A rolls back, B's insert goes through. Either way, one row. The stepper below plays it frame by frame.

Catching that error is clumsy. An error spoils the whole transaction it happens in, until it's rolled back. A worker that stores 500 messages in one transaction loses all 500 to a single repeat.

INSERT ... ON CONFLICT (payment_uid) DO NOTHING moves the decision into the statement itself. The insert asks the unique index in the same step as the write. If the code is already there, or is being inserted by a transaction that hasn't finished (it waits for that one first), the insert skips the row instead of failing. Add RETURNING payment_id, which hands back columns of the rows the statement wrote, and you learn which happened: one row back means the payment was new, none means it was a repeat. The stepper shows it holding up in every order of events.

On paper, two waiters who each check the order book, find nothing and then write make our workers' mistake. A unique index is a book where checking and writing are one movement of one pen. The picture breaks on speed: a pen serves one writer at a time, while PostgreSQL lets thousands of inserts with different codes through at once.

A check in a separate statement can be out of date before you act on it. Let the unique index decide.

But some second messages carry news, and should change the row. Next, we'll handle those.

try.title: Race two inserts
steps: Open two terminals in the labs folder and run psql in both: docker compose -f env/postgres.yml exec db psql -U sfz -d course. Call them A and B. Each is one session, an open connection to the database, like one of our two workers. Start the database first if it isn't running (docker compose -f env/postgres.yml up -d --wait).

sections.h: When the second message should change the row: ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE
sections.html:
Not every repeat is a copy. A card payment happens in two steps. First the card's bank says yes and sets the money aside, and the payment is stored as pending. Later the money really moves, and a second message arrives with the same code and the status succeeded, or failed if it never moved. Payment 20 in the seed is still pending. When its second message arrives, the conflict should update the row, not skip it:

INSERT INTO payments AS p (payment_uid, card_id, merchant_id, amount_minor, status, created_at)
VALUES ('019d0ab9-28c0-7014-8000-000000000014', 3, 1, 7425, 'succeeded', '2026-03-20 10:10+00')
ON CONFLICT (payment_uid) DO UPDATE
SET status = EXCLUDED.status
WHERE p.status = 'pending' AND EXCLUDED.status <> 'pending'
RETURNING p.payment_id, old.status AS old_status, new.status AS new_status;

AS p gives the table a short name. EXCLUDED is the row the INSERT proposed and couldn't insert, so SET status = EXCLUDED.status copies the new message's status onto the stored row. The WHERE decides whether the stored row changes at all. An insert that turns into an update when the row already exists is called an upsert.

Why the WHERE? Messages can arrive late and out of order. Without it, a late pending message, one that arrives after the succeeded one, would set a finished payment back to pending. With it, only a pending payment moves (p.status = 'pending'), and only to a final status (<> means "is not"). Any other repeat leaves the row alone and returns nothing.

RETURNING old.status, new.status is new in PostgreSQL 18: old is the row before the statement and new the row after. For a fresh insert, old is all NULL, the value SQL uses for "nothing here". For an update, both are filled. So one statement tells the worker what it did: inserted, updated, or nothing. The PostgreSQL manual promises an insert or an update here "even under high concurrency", with many writers at once.

Three rules decide whether the statement works at all:

  • The conflict target, (payment_uid), must name a column with a unique index or a UNIQUE rule. A clash on any other unique index, such as the one on payment_id, still raises an error.
  • One statement may not change the same row twice. A batch that carries one code twice fails with ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE command cannot affect row a second time, so remove the repeats from the batch first.
  • payment_id comes from a sequence, a counter inside the database that hands out the next number. Every insert that is tried takes a number, including the ones that end in a conflict. So the ids get gaps, and you can't use them as a count.

DO UPDATE has one more cost. PostgreSQL never changes a row in place: an UPDATE writes a new copy of the row and marks the old one dead, even when the values are the same. The WHERE saves those writes too. (The Transactions track's lesson MVCC: versions, snapshots and VACUUM explains why.)

ON CONFLICT handles messages as they arrive. A nightly job that corrects a whole table needs one more tool. Next, we'll meet it.

sections.h: Bringing a table of totals up to date in one statement: MERGE
sections.html:
Shop owners want to see what they've taken each month. Adding up every payment on every visit would be slow, so the app keeps a summary table, merchant_month_totals, with one row per shop per month: the shop, the month, the total of its succeeded payments in cents (gross_minor) and how many there were (payment_count). Every night, a job works the totals out again from the payments and brings the table up to date.

Since the last run, three things can have happened to a month. A shop's first payment came in: a row to insert. A late payment arrived: a row to correct. A payment turned out to have failed, and the shop has no sales left that month: a row to delete. ON CONFLICT can insert and update, but it can't delete. MERGE does all three in one statement:

MERGE INTO merchant_month_totals AS t
USING (SELECT merchant_id, date '2026-02-01' AS month,
              sum(amount_minor) AS gross_minor, count(*) AS payment_count
       FROM payments
       WHERE status = 'succeeded' AND created_at >= '2026-02-01' AND created_at < '2026-03-01'
       GROUP BY merchant_id) AS s
ON t.merchant_id = s.merchant_id AND t.month = s.month
WHEN MATCHED AND (t.gross_minor, t.payment_count) IS DISTINCT FROM (s.gross_minor, s.payment_count) THEN
    UPDATE SET gross_minor = s.gross_minor, payment_count = s.payment_count
WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN
    INSERT VALUES (s.merchant_id, s.month, s.gross_minor, s.payment_count)
WHEN NOT MATCHED BY SOURCE AND t.month = date '2026-02-01' THEN
    DELETE
RETURNING merge_action(), t.merchant_id, old.gross_minor, new.gross_minor;

The part after USING is the source: a query that works out February's totals from the payments. GROUP BY merchant_id makes one row per shop, and sum and count add up that shop's payments. MERGE lines up the target table with the source on the ON condition, here the same shop and month, and puts every row into one of three classes. MATCHED rows are on both sides. NOT MATCHED rows are only in the source. NOT MATCHED BY SOURCE rows are only in the target; that class came in PostgreSQL 17.

For each row, the first WHEN clause whose class and extra condition fit decides what happens. The extra condition on MATCHED uses IS DISTINCT FROM, which means "differs", with NULL treated as an ordinary value. So a matched row whose numbers already agree fits no clause and is left alone. On paper, this is someone at closing time with the totals page and the day's receipts: write in the shop that's missing, correct the wrong total, cross out the month with no sales left.

Mind the condition on the DELETE. The source holds February only, so every January row is "not matched by source" too. Leave out AND t.month = ... and the MERGE deletes all of January, which nobody asked for, as the Try it shows. RETURNING on MERGE, with merge_action() to say which branch produced each row, came in PostgreSQL 17, and PostgreSQL 18 added old and new. If two source rows match the same target row, MERGE fails with MERGE command cannot affect row a second time.

MERGE has one weakness, and it's the opening's problem again. It sorts rows into MATCHED and NOT MATCHED from the data it sees when it starts, and nothing makes it wait for another session's unfinished insert of the same key. When two sessions (open connections to the database, like our two workers) merge the same new shop and month at once, both choose INSERT, and the second fails with 23505. The PostgreSQL manual points to ON CONFLICT for that case.

MERGE syncs a table from a source, one job at a time. Messages that can arrive twice at once go through ON CONFLICT.

That's the limit of today's tools: each is safe only for the writer it was built for. And we typed every statement into psql by hand. A real program sends its own SQL, and that has costs of its own.

opening:
Picture a café on a busy morning. You tap your card, and the card reader sends a message about the payment to the company that records it. The reader hears nothing back, so it sends the same message again. Both copies arrive a millisecond apart, and two copies of the company's program pick up one each. Each asks the database, "do we have this payment yet?" Each hears no, and each stores it. You've paid for one coffee twice.

Looking before you write feels like the careful thing to do. It's what you'd do with a paper order book, and it passes every test, because a test sends one message at a time.

The last lesson, LATERAL joins, top-N per group and keyset pagination, only read rows; this one writes them. We'll store the loose notes that come with each payment as a JSON document and search inside it, store a message that arrives twice exactly once, and update a table of monthly totals in one statement. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.
closing:
We started with a café customer charged twice for one coffee, because two workers each looked before they wrote. Looking first can't work when the answer changes between the look and the write. The unique index decides at the moment of the write, so with ON CONFLICT the repeat is stored as nothing.

Next time a checkout page warns you not to press Pay twice, you've found a system without that referee. A careful one would let you press it ten times and charge you once.

Next, we'll leave psql and send SQL from a program, and find out why storing 2,000 payments one at a time is slow while the database sits idle.

compare.title: Storing one payment message safely: Oracle and PostgreSQL

a.label: Oracle
a.title: Oracle: MERGE is the upsert
a.html: MERGE INTO payments p USING (SELECT :uid AS payment_uid, :card AS card_id, :merchant AS merchant_id, :amount AS amount_minor, :status AS status, :created AS created_at FROM dual) m ON (p.payment_uid = m.payment_uid) WHEN MATCHED THEN UPDATE SET p.status = m.status WHERE p.status = 'pending' AND m.status <> 'pending' WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN INSERT (payment_uid, card_id, merchant_id, amount_minor, status, created_at) VALUES (m.payment_uid, m.card_id, m.merchant_id, m.amount_minor, m.status, m.created_at); -- two sessions inserting the same new uid at once: -- the second can fail with ORA-00001; catch and retry

b.label: PostgreSQL 18
b.title: PostgreSQL: INSERT ... ON CONFLICT
b.html: INSERT INTO payments AS p (payment_uid, card_id, merchant_id, amount_minor, status, created_at) VALUES (:uid, :card, :merchant, :amount, :status, :created) ON CONFLICT (payment_uid) DO UPDATE SET status = EXCLUDED.status WHERE p.status = 'pending' AND EXCLUDED.status <> 'pending' RETURNING p.payment_id, old.status, new.status; -- a concurrent insert of the same uid makes this -- one wait, then take the DO UPDATE branch: -- no error to catch

compare.note: Oracle Database is a commercial database program that many banks run. It has no ON CONFLICT clause, so Oracle code writes the upsert as a MERGE whose source is a single row, often taken from dual, Oracle's built-in table of one row. PostgreSQL has MERGE too, since version 15, and with the same race: MERGE decides MATCHED or NOT MATCHED before it writes, so two MERGEs of the same new key at once can both choose INSERT, and the unique index rejects the second (ORA-00001 is Oracle's duplicate key error). INSERT ... ON CONFLICT is different, because the unique index decides inside the write: the second session waits for the first, then takes the DO UPDATE or DO NOTHING branch, with no error to catch. The WHERE on the update branch exists in both and does the same job: a late message never moves a payment backward. PostgreSQL 18 adds RETURNING old and new to both statements, and Oracle 23ai added them for UPDATE and MERGE.

worked.title: Storing a batch of 500 messages in one statement

steps.say: Real workers don't take messages one at a time. Say the messages come from Kafka, a program that keeps a long list of messages and lets other programs read them in order, and our worker reads 500 at a time (records). Some may repeat each other, because the card reader sent them again. Some may repeat payments already stored, and some bring the final status of a pending payment. First, keep one message per code, preferring a final status over pending, because one statement may not touch the same row twice:
steps.code: // 1. one message per uid; a final status beats 'pending' val batch = records.map { it.value() } // List<PaymentMessage> .sortedByDescending { it.status != "pending" } // final statuses first .distinctBy { it.uid } // keeps the first of each uid

steps.say: Send the whole batch as six arrays, one per column, and let unnest turn them back into rows inside the database. An array here is a list of values sent as one parameter, one ?. That's one statement and one trip across the network for 500 messages, instead of 500. The ON CONFLICT clause is the one from this lesson.
steps.code: -- 2. the statement: unnest turns six arrays into rows INSERT INTO payments AS p (payment_uid, card_id, merchant_id, amount_minor, status, created_at) SELECT * FROM unnest(?::uuid[], ?::bigint[], ?::bigint[], ?::bigint[], ?::text[], ?::timestamptz[]) ON CONFLICT (payment_uid) DO UPDATE SET status = EXCLUDED.status WHERE p.status = 'pending' AND EXCLUDED.status <> 'pending' RETURNING p.payment_id, old.status, new.status

steps.say: Bind each column as an array through JDBC, the standard library that Java and Kotlin programs use to talk to a database (the next lesson opens it up). The rows that come back are exactly the changes: an insert has a NULL old status, a payment that moved on has pending, and repeats return nothing.
steps.code: // 3. bind the arrays and read what changed val changes = conn.prepareStatement(UPSERT_BATCH).use { ps -> ps.setArray(1, conn.createArrayOf("uuid", batch.map { it.uid }.toTypedArray())) ps.setArray(2, conn.createArrayOf("bigint", batch.map { it.cardId }.toTypedArray())) ps.setArray(3, conn.createArrayOf("bigint", batch.map { it.merchantId }.toTypedArray())) ps.setArray(4, conn.createArrayOf("bigint", batch.map { it.amountMinor }.toTypedArray())) ps.setArray(5, conn.createArrayOf("text", batch.map { it.status }.toTypedArray())) ps.setArray(6, conn.createArrayOf("timestamptz", batch.map { Timestamp.from(it.createdAt) }.toTypedArray())) ps.executeQuery().use { rs -> buildList { while (rs.next()) add(Change(rs.getLong(1), rs.getString(2), rs.getString(3))) } } }

steps.say: Save the payments first, and tell Kafka the batch is done second (consumer is the worker's link to Kafka). If the worker dies between the two lines, Kafka hands it the same batch again, and the upsert turns every message in it into a no-op, a statement that changes nothing. Messages that arrive at least once, plus a write that's safe to repeat, store each payment exactly once.
steps.code: // 4. order of the two commits conn.commit() // the payments are durable consumer.commitSync() // only now tell Kafka the batch is done // a crash between the two lines: the batch comes back, and every row in it // hits ON CONFLICT and changes nothing

drill.title: The ingest statement, from memory
drill.prompt: Without looking, write the statement that stores one payment message (code, card, shop, amount, status, created_at) so that a repeat changes nothing, a final status moves a pending payment, a late 'pending' never moves a payment backward, and the statement reports whether it inserted, updated or did nothing. Then write the query for the payments whose fraud rules include "geo_mismatch" (a card used far from where it usually is), in a form a GIN index on metadata can serve.

answer.html: INSERT INTO payments AS p (payment_uid, card_id, merchant_id, amount_minor, status, created_at) VALUES ($1, $2, $3, $4, $5, $6) ON CONFLICT (payment_uid) DO UPDATE -- the unique index decides, even mid-race SET status = EXCLUDED.status -- EXCLUDED: the row the INSERT proposed WHERE p.status = 'pending' -- only pending payments move, AND EXCLUDED.status <> 'pending' -- and only forward RETURNING p.payment_id, old.status AS old_status, -- NULL: inserted new.status AS new_status; -- no row at all: a repeat SELECT payment_id FROM payments WHERE metadata @> '{"risk": {"rules": ["geo_mismatch"]}}'; -- containment: GIN can answer it -- payments 8 and 31 on the seed

recap: A jsonb column parses a JSON document once, when it's stored, refuses broken ones, and lets SQL look inside: -> returns jsonb, ->> returns text. Text compares letter by letter, so turn a number back into a number (::int) before you compare it.

@> asks whether a document contains a smaller one. A GIN index lists every key and value with the rows that hold it, like the index at the back of a book, so containment reads only the matching rows. Conditions written with ->> can't use it.

Check, then insert, is a race: two workers can both find nothing and both insert. The unique index is the referee, and INSERT ... ON CONFLICT asks it in the same step as the write, so a repeat waits, then does nothing instead of failing.

ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE SET status = EXCLUDED.status WHERE ... turns a second message with news into an update, and the WHERE stops a late message from moving a payment backward. PostgreSQL 18's RETURNING old and new says what happened. One statement can't touch the same row twice.
MERGE inserts, updates and deletes against a source in one statement. Guard its DELETE, or it removes every row the source doesn't mention.
The limit: MERGE isn't safe when two sessions write the same new key at once, and ON CONFLICT can't delete. Use ON CONFLICT for messages that may arrive twice, and MERGE for one nightly job.

explain.prompt: A teammate's worker stores payments with if (repo.findByUid(uid) == null) repo.insert(msg), inside one transaction per batch of messages. It passes every test, but about once a week a batch fails with a duplicate key error and has to be run again. Explain what's happening and what you'd change.
explain.answer: The weekly failure is two deliveries of the same message overlapping. The card reader or the network sent a message again, and the copy reached a second worker while the first was still storing it. Each worker's transaction runs its findByUid before the other has committed, so both see nothing and both insert. The UNIQUE rule on payment_uid catches it: the second insert waits for the first transaction, then fails with 23505. The error spoils that worker's whole transaction, so it loses the whole batch and has to run it again. Without the UNIQUE rule, the payment would quietly be stored twice. Tests never show this, because they send one message at a time. I'd remove the check and let the insert ask the unique index itself: INSERT ... ON CONFLICT (payment_uid) DO NOTHING, or DO UPDATE SET status = EXCLUDED.status WHERE the stored payment is still pending and the message carries a final status, with RETURNING to learn whether it inserted, updated or did nothing. The second worker then waits and takes the conflict branch instead of failing. I'd also remove repeated codes from each batch before sending it, since one statement may not touch the same row twice, and mark the batch as done only after the database commit, so a crash in between means the batch is harmlessly sent again.

deeper.html:
DO NOTHING doesn't return the existing row, so a caller that needs the id of a repeat has to ask again: SELECT payment_id FROM payments WHERE payment_uid = $1. A common workaround is DO UPDATE SET status = p.status, an update that changes nothing so that RETURNING has a row, but it writes a new copy of the row on every repeat. PostgreSQL 19, at release candidate as this lesson is written, is set to add ON CONFLICT DO SELECT, which hands the existing row to RETURNING without writing a new copy. Check the final release notes before you rely on it.

ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE locks the conflicting row while it updates it, so upserts of one key from many sessions queue up one behind the other. That's what you want for a final status racing its own repeat. It also means that a very busy key, such as a single counter row that every request upserts, becomes a queue. The Transactions track's lesson Lost updates: row locks, SKIP LOCKED and job queues covers those waits.

Before PostgreSQL 18 there was no old in RETURNING, and people told inserts from updates with RETURNING (xmax = 0) AS inserted. xmax is a hidden column on every row that records the transaction that deleted or replaced it, so a freshly inserted row has none. It works, but it leans on an internal detail. Use old on 18.

PostgreSQL 17 brought the SQL standard's JSON functions. JSON_TABLE turns a document into rows and typed columns inside FROM, the standard spelling of what the last lesson did with jsonb_array_elements_text:

SELECT p.payment_id, r.rule
FROM payments p,
     JSON_TABLE(p.metadata, '$.risk.rules[*]' COLUMNS (rule text PATH '$')) AS r
ORDER BY p.payment_id;
-- 3 velocity, 8 geo_mismatch, 15 velocity, 18 velocity, 31 geo_mismatch

jsonpath, the small query language inside that '$.risk.rules[*]', also works with the @? operator: metadata @? '$.risk.score ? (@ > 50)' finds the same 8 payments as the cast, and a GIN index can serve it.

A GIN index comes in a second, smaller flavour. If you only ever ask with @>, USING gin (metadata jsonb_path_ops) builds an index of 4.5 MB on the big table, about half the default. It serves @>, @? and @@, but not the operators that ask whether a key exists.

A unique index on an expression works as a conflict target too. For email addresses compared without regard to capital letters, CREATE UNIQUE INDEX ON customers (lower(email)) and then ON CONFLICT ((lower(email))) DO NOTHING.
